doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Metronome folds; Jazz magazine for Bob Thiele
summary: Why Metronome closed, the publisher's own jazz history, and Morgenstern's unpaid editing of Bob Thiele's Jazz magazine, paid in liner notes.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: changed his tax picture so he could no longer write the magazine off. And that’s when he came to us and said — because he was an ex-musician. He had been a tenor and clarinet player in the twenties, and he actually — I found out, I made a correction to Brian Rust’s famous Discography because he was listed as unknown in the personnel, to a very obscure band called Dunk Rendleman and his Alabamians that recorded for Gennett in 1926 or something. But I was able to tell Brian that the gentleman named Robert Asen was the unknown clarinet and tenor. So he, you know, he was a nice guy and he really had a feeling for the music and everything, but he had to close the magazine down. And then the next thing for me after collecting unemployment and translating Joe Baron’s jazz book, that was a welcome little thing there. Bob Thiele, the noted producer, mostly known for his association with John Coltrane of course, it started — he had a magazine when he was a kid. He was a rich kid. His father had Baker’s Chocolate, and he started a magazine called Jazz in 1941 and then it folded in 1942 because I think he was drafted into the Coast Guard. That’s when he had already started Signature. He was like a wunderkind deal. But then he got the yen to start a magazine again, but because he was working for Impulse he didn’t want his name associated with it. And I became the first unpaid editor of this magazine called Jazz, which eventually became “Jazz and Pop,” but that was after I had left. But he paid me off in liner notes and they paid better. They paid 75 bucks rather than 30 something.
